summary: The animations.dev home page is the sales page for Emil Kowalski's paid web animation course, so it mostly outlines what the course teaches rather than teaching it. Its core argument is that code alone does not make an animation work: a bad easing or duration can ruin an otherwise great animation, and a great animation comes from choosing the right ingredients, namely the easing, the duration and which properties to animate so it stays performant. The course structure doubles as a checklist for a design system's motion work: know why some animations feel better, how to choose easing and duration, when to use springs, when not to animate at all, and how to use AI; then implement with CSS first and Motion (formerly Framer Motion) second, and finally move from good to great through orchestration, conveying feeling, accessibility and performance. It also names Emil's credentials (Linear, Vercel's design system, and the Sonner and Vaul libraries) and lists the 15 AI skills bundled with the course.
key_ideas: Code alone does not make an animation work; a bad easing or duration can ruin an otherwise great animation.
A great animation is built from known ingredients: the right easing, the right duration, and the right properties to animate so it stays performant.
Knowing the ingredients replaces guessing ('Does this easing work?', 'Is this enter transition too long?') with confident choices.
Many tutorials, and Framer Motion's own documentation, follow a happy path and do not show how to build complex animations or what to do when something breaks.
Animation theory covers easing, spring animations, timing, purpose and taste, including when you should not animate.
Which easing and duration you chose, and why, is often more important than the code itself.
Get CSS animations right first (transforms, transitions, keyframes) so moving to Motion is easy.
Going from good to great involves conveying feelings through animation, orchestration, accessibility and performance.
Build animations by first thinking and talking about the animation you want, then coding, improving and iterating.
The Dynamic Island walkthrough uses spring animation to make the motion feel organic and natural.
Animation theory applies beyond code: to prototypes, designs and anywhere else.
Animations on the web can be treated as a form of art, with care for how they look, feel and behave, aiming for a moment of joy.

caveats: This is a sales page for a paid, closed course; it lists what the course teaches but not the lessons' actual values or curves (for example the custom easing curves are mentioned but not given).

Most of the page (roughly lines 59-289) is customer testimonials; they are marketing, and techniques they mention in passing (an auto-height tip, useMeasure for smooth resizing) are not explained, so they are not turned into rules.
Endorsements from Benji Taylor, Una and Matt Perry are praise, not guidance.
Pricing, discounts, PPP, refunds, invoices, certificate, Discord and team licences are product details, not design guidance.
The page is internally inconsistent on cadence: the FAQ says there are 4 enrollment periods a year, while the header says the next enrollment opens in 2027 for 10 days.
The changelog says the theory module had 7 lessons; this page says 8 (possibly after the Practical Animation Tips lesson was added [inferred]).
The 15 AI skills are part of the paid course; their names are listed but their contents are not on this page.
The Family drawer walkthrough uses 'Visual components by Family', marked 'For educational purposes only'; its craft can inform a system, but its visual identity is Family's and must not be reused.
The 90,000,000 weekly npm downloads for Sonner and Vaul is the page's own figure, not verified here.
